(advanced) sequencing strategy guide:
Your Upload Strategy is killing your YouTube channel.
No one really looks into it, but the order in which you release your videos matters A LOT.
Here’s why sequencing matters:
When a viewer finishes your new video, YouTube asks “what should we show them next?”
If you’ve uploaded in a random order, the next video they watch might be completely irrelevant,
and the viewer leaves the platform.
That’s a negative signal for your channel.
But if your uploads are connected, the next recommendation makes sense, and the viewer
keeps binge watching your channel.
This is called content chaining.
Each video should be a stepping stone to another, guiding the viewer deeper into your world.
When you post in the right order, you create a binge-watching loop that YouTube loves because
it increases time on the platform.
More time spent on YouTube = more ads = more push for your videos.
Poor sequencing breaks this chain.
Example: you post a video on “Beginner Camera Settings,” then your next upload is “The
History of Film Editing,” then “Top 10 YouTubers in 2024.”
Made by NotNotAbu2
Made by NotNotAbu2
Your audience and the algorithm have no idea where you’re going.
The same even applies if you're doing external monetization.
Say you're running a business channel and you make a top-of-the-funnel video that gets tons of
views. A lot of the viewers will then look for a more advanced video that goes into depths of
whatever you're teaching before buying your product.
But if they can't find that video on your channel, they lose trust and they won't end up buying
your product. That means you just missed out on tons of revenue because you decided to
release a TOF video before something that goes more detailed.
Think about video ladders. A video ladder is a planned sequence where each upload builds on
the last:
1. Intro-level topic to attract a broad audience
2. Follow-up that goes deeper into the same topic
3. Advanced video for the most engaged viewers
This way, each upload sends relevant, high-quality traffic to the next.
And the next video should already exist on your channel.
The compounding effect of good sequencing:
> The algorithm starts taking your channel seriously
> Your watch time is high because the audience has tons of relevant things to watch
> Time spent on YouTube increases, which makes YouTube promote you harder
So here's how to fix your upload strategy:
1. Decide the logical viewing order before filming
2. Use end screens, pinned comments, and playlists to guide viewers
3. Always know what your next video will be before you post the current one
TL;DR: upload order matters more than you think. Random videos break binge-watching chains
and kill momentum, while sequenced uploads build a natural flow that keeps viewers watching.
Use video ladders that start broad, go deeper, and then target your most engaged viewers. The
goal is to increase session time so YouTube rewards you with more promotion.
[[PAGE 2]]
100x impressions cheat code guide
YouTube doesn’t care about your video.
It only cares about how people respond to it.
That’s why your "great" video gets ignored.
Most creators think their job is to make the best video possible, so they obsess over editing,
scriptwriting, gear, color grading, transitions and everything else under the sun.
They're all important things to focus on, but none of it matters if no one clicks.
Because YouTube doesn't push the best edited video. It pushes what gets clicked and watched.
That’s why packaging (title + thumbnail) is the real game.
Your title and thumbnail do more to decide your video’s success than the content inside.
If the packaging doesn’t spark curiosity, promise value, trigger emotion, or FORCE the viewer to
click on it, even the best video in the world won’t get views.
Here’s what you ACTUALLY need to do:
Made by NotNotAbu2
Made by NotNotAbu2
1. Research before you create
Before filming, go to YouTube, search the topic you’re making a video on, and find the answer to
these questions:
> What type of titles are they using?
> What do the top-ranking thumbnails look like?
> Is there a pattern in the wording, colors, or emotions?
This matters so you stop guessing what works (where 99% of the time you're wrong) and
instead you can reverse-engineer what is already succeeding.
2. Use proven title formats
There are tons of title formats that are all over YouTube, and these formats basically 10x-1000x
the chances of your video succeeding.
You can research general YouTube to find title formats but the best place to start is your niche
and competitors.
Example of some title formats:
> $1 vs $1,000,000 {thing}
> The BEST {topic} Strategy In {year}
> The ONLY {topic} You'll Ever Need
3. Use proven thumbnail styles
Just like there are certain title formats that work way better than others, there are also certain
thumbnail styles that work better than others.
Make sure you do proper research within your niche to see what's working and what types of
thumbnails people are clicking on.
4. Optimize the first 10 seconds of your video
If your title promises something, make sure the intro immediately confirms it. Viewers clicked for
a reason, so you have to validate their decision ASAP.
Don’t waste 20 seconds with your logo or “Hey guys, welcome back...”
TL;DR: If nobody’s clicking, your video might as well not exist. So it's your job to make the video
impossible to ignore. People MUST click on your video to even get to the content, so incentivize
them to click.
Exposing MrBeast for being a copycat guide
YouTube loves copycats.
[[PAGE 3]]
Every big creator on YouTube is copying someone else, and they're all being rewarded by
YouTube.
Almost every new creator falls into the same trap of thinking the best way to grow is to “be
different.” They want to invent a completely new style of content, an editing format no one has
seen before, or an entirely new niche.
But there's a MASSIVE problem with this approach.
It's that YouTube doesn’t care about originality, it cares about proof. The algorithm doesn’t take
risks on untested formats. It plays favorites with what already works. If you look around, the
biggest channels didn’t win because they invented something brand new. They won because
they took proven ideas and executed them better.
Just take a look at MrBeast. Everyone knows him as the biggest innovator on YouTube. But was
he really the first to do challenges? No. Challenges existed long before him.
What made him stand out was scale and execution. He looked at formats that were already like
the last person to leave, survival challenges, game-style competitions and simply did it on a
bigger budget, with higher stakes, and cleaner packaging.
That’s copying strategically.
Same thing with Dream, he wasn’t the first Minecraft creator. He wasn’t even the first to do
“manhunt” type videos. But he saw the power of that idea, turned it into a repeatable format and
Made by NotNotAbu2
Made by NotNotAbu2
optimized everything from pacing, to commentary, to thumbnail storytelling until manhunts
became his format.
He didn’t reinvent anything new, he just refined and scaled it.
Alex Hormozi was also not the first person teaching online business. His entire video strategy is
modeled on what already works in short, direct, educational content. Clean thumbnails, direct
delivery, data-backed titles and repackaged value.
He just produces it at scale with relentless consistency.
Again, it’s not new, it’s strategic copying with his own twist.
So here's what you need to understand, innovating on YouTube is a huge gamble, and you have
99% chances of losing.
Viewers want the videos to be entertaining, engaging, and easy to consume.
Proven formats already check those boxes, so just replicate them, don't make your job harder.
This is why you constantly see waves of almost identical videos dominating at once. A certain
title formula blows up, and suddenly dozens of creators copy it. A thumbnail design goes viral,
then your entire feed is filled with versions of it.
It’s not an accident. It’s the algorithm showing that people want more of that exact thing.
Creators who rush to replicate are simply feeding the demand. Creators who resist and try to be
original get left behind.
Made by NotNotAbu2
Made by NotNotAbu2
So ask yourself:
> What topics create repeatable success?
> What title formats show up again and again?
> What thumbnails are getting clicked most in my niche?
> How do the top 1% creators hook viewers in the first 30 seconds?
Let’s break this down into practical steps you can take right now to copy like a pro without
feeling like a fraud:
[[PAGE 4]]
Step 1. Build A Watchlist
Pick the top 5–10 direct competitors in your niche. Create a system to track them (Notion,
Google Sheet, whatever works).
Every time they upload, log the title, thumbnail style, topic, and performance. Over time,
patterns will emerge and you’ll see exactly what’s clicking with viewers.
Step 2: Look For Outliers
Don’t just copy everything. Look at their last 20 uploads and isolate the 2–3 that significantly
outperformed the rest. Those are the outliers.
Ask yourself why those worked. Was it the packaging? The topic? The stakes? The format
length? This is where you’ll find which part of the video actually made the difference.
Made by NotNotAbu2
Made by NotNotAbu2
Step 3: Create A Bank
Every time you see a successful format or title, add it to a “bank”. This is your personal swipe
file of proven YouTube content.
Over weeks and months, you’ll build a massive list of ideas with actual evidence that they work.
When you need your next video idea, you don't need to spend hours, you can pull from the
bank.
Step 4: Put Your Own Spin On It
This is the part where people misunderstand copycat strategy. You don’t carbon copy. You take
the skeleton of the format and make your own version. Change the context, add your
personality, raise the stakes, shift the angle.
For example: if your competitor did “Surviving 24 Hours With Only $1,” maybe you do “Surviving
48 Hours With Only $1 In [specific country]” It’s familiar enough for viewers to click, but unique
enough to be yours.
Step 5: Execute consistently
You should now be doing this for all of your new uploads. You have to feed the algorithm what it
already knows people want until you become the authority in your space. That’s how you win
long term.
Some people will still resist. They'll say “I don’t want to be like everyone else”.
Here’s the irony is that everyone they look up to had to blend in first and copy other people
before they could stand out.
Once you’ve built leverage, once you’ve become the niche leader, then you can experiment and
innovate. Until then, put your ego down and start replicating what's already working.
TL;DR: YouTube doesn't like innovation, nor do your viewers. So you have to copy strategically
by studying your competitors, tracking what works, building your own personal swipe file, adding
your own twists into the videos and consistently repeating the process.
That is how EVERYONE else succeeded on YouTube, and that's the only way you can succeed.
Why your youtube videos dont get views guide
YouTube hates you.
That is the reason your channel isn’t growing.
PS: YouTube doesn’t literally hate you, but it also has no reason to be on your side. Whereas
there are creators like MrBeast whom YouTube treats like royalty.
And the reason for that is because channels like MrBeast have years of data showing they can
pull millions of people in, keep them hooked for the entire video, and drive massive ad revenue.
YouTube has an invisible ranking system (it's a lot more complicated than that, but for the sake
of understanding, let's just say it's a ranking system).
[[PAGE 5]]
Every channel starts at the bottom. When you upload, YouTube will quietly test your video with a
tiny audience to see how people respond. If those early viewers click and stay, you’ll get more
reach. If they don’t, distribution dies quickly. In the early stages, the algorithm assumes nothing
about you. You have to earn every inch of trust.
The only way to climb that ranking is to prove that your channel helps YouTube achieve its
single biggest goal, which is keeping people on the platform for as long as possible so they can
watch more ads. That’s it. YouTube does not care about making creators happy, it only cares
about making more money.
There are 5 important pillars that you must abide by to get high up in YouTube's ranking:
Made by NotNotAbu2
Made by NotNotAbu2
Pillar 1: Consistent high-quality uploads
This doesn’t mean daily posting, it means a predictable output of videos that hold people’s
attention for a long time.
And all of your videos must do the same, you cannot have highly successful videos and then
extremely underperforming videos, that sends a mixed signal to YouTube. It will be a gamble for
YouTube to push your video when there is a high risk of the video not keeping viewers' attention
to the end. And YouTube doesn't want to gamble, it wants total
Pillar 2: Watch time
Getting people to click is the 1st step, but it doesn't really mean anything if people leave after 20
seconds. YouTube looks at the average watch time of your video compared to similar videos in
the same niche. If you’re holding viewers longer than your competitors, you’re proving you can
keep the audience engaged as that's exactly what YouTube wants.
Pillar 3: Being real
YouTube’s systems track your account’s behavior outside of uploads too. If you watch and
engage with other content in your niche, you’re helping YouTube understand where to position
your channel in the ecosystem. A channel that behaves like part of a community has a clearer
“profile” for the algorithm to work with.
Pillar 4: Do not kill trust
Nothing destroys your standing with YouTube faster than misleading packaging. If you use
clickbait titles and thumbnails that don’t match the video’s content, people will click off in the first
few seconds. That tells YouTube your content loses attention, which is the exact opposite of
what it’s looking for.
YouTube takes this very seriously, and often just terminates channels that use misleading
packaging without any warning.
Pillar 5: Doubling down on winners
When a video starts performing above your average, it’s a signal that you’ve hit on something
valuable. The fastest way to build trust is to replicate that success with newer videos that appeal
to the same audience. This shows YouTube you can deliver repeatedly, and one day it will start
trusting you like it trusts MrBeast.
TL;DR: YouTube has an invisible ranking system. You start at the very bottom and you have to
work your way up if you want to grow. And to do that, you must follow these 5 pillars:
Youtube business model, explained guide
YouTube is using you.
And you're at a massive disadvantage even if you don't realize yet.
YouTube’s entire business model depends on creators pumping out content that keeps people
on the platform for as long as possible.
[[PAGE 6]]
The longer viewers stay, the more ads YouTube can run, and the more money YouTube makes.
Very simple.
Creators are the engine for that system. Your job is to keep viewers watching for longer
sessions so the ad machine never stops.
The problem? YouTube needs you to keep the machine running, but it has no obligation to you.
They give you a small cut of the ad revenue and in exchange, they have all the power.
> You don’t get a direct relationship with your audience.
> You don’t actually control where your content is distributed.
The worst part is that you have NO security.
Your channel can be terminated without warning for reasons you can’t control.
One copyright claim, one community guidelines strike, one “policy update” can destroy your
years of work, millions of views and your entire audience.
Made by NotNotAbu2
Made by NotNotAbu2
There’s no appeal process that guarantees you get it back. There's no safety net for you to fall
back on.
And because the system is so unforgiving, creators are pressured into chasing metrics at all
costs.
They start optimizing for clickbait, they build videos around manufactured tension, fake drama,
and watch traps that do nothing for the viewer but keep them “engaged” in YouTube’s eyes.
This is why creators end up making content that they don't necessarily want to, because the
system rewards tactics that keep people on the platform at any cost.
So here's the mindset shift you need: YouTube is not your business.
Do not depend on YouTube for everything. Just use it as a distribution channel.
The fix is to start building your own ecosystem in parallel.
> Collect emails so you can contact your audience directly, even if your channel disappears.
> Build a community space you control. It can be a Discord server, a newsletter, a paid group.
> Create a product, service, or offer that gives your viewers what they want, and make it the
natural next step after watching your videos.
By doing this, the algorithm stops being a life-or-death factor for your income. You won't be
affected by random CPM drops keeping you up at night.
If YouTube changes its rules or tanks your reach, your revenue will not be affected because you
own the audience and have a direct way to serve and sell to them.
Now, you are using YouTube instead of YouTube using you.
P.S: I want to clarify that YouTube isn't necessarily evil for this. It's just the business model. Now
the responsibility is on you as a creator to not be taken advantage of and to play the game of
YouTube in a way that will benefit you. And relying on YouTube AdSense will not benefit you in
any way.
Youtube doesnt care about hard work - guide
YouTube doesn't care about hard work.
Have you ever spent 50 hours making a video, perfecting every edit and designing a nice
thumbnail, only for it to get 200 views?
People think effort = success.
But that couldn't be further away from the truth. YouTube doesn’t care about your late nights or
how many edits you made.
YouTube only cares about one thing: how people respond.
If your video doesn’t get clicked, doesn’t hold attention, and doesn’t make people want to watch
more, the effort doesn't matter.
[[PAGE 7]]
These videos are pretty low effort, but they've gotten millions of views:
Made by NotNotAbu2
Made by NotNotAbu2
So, what does YouTube actually reward?
1. Watch time
2. Strong idea
3. Consistency of quality
1. Watch time
This is everything YouTube cares about. If you can hold attention longer than other videos,
YouTube pushes you harder.
Why? Because the longer people watch, the more ads YouTube can show, and that means
more money for them.
At the end of the day, YouTube only cares about making money. So if your videos help YouTube
do that, they’ll reward you by pushing your content to more viewers.
The best way to get YouTube on your side is to make videos that keep people watching longer.
2. Strong idea
No one clicks on your video because it's in high resolution or because of expensive gear. They
click because of the idea behind it.
You could film paint drying and if that idea makes people curious enough, they’ll click.
Unfortunately this is where most people fail. They focus on execution and forget packaging.
Made by NotNotAbu2
Made by NotNotAbu2
Execution is definitely important, don't get me wrong, but obsessing over the editing and
completely ignoring whether anyone even cares about the topic in the first place is a waste of
time.
3. Consistency of Quality
By "quality", I don't mean 4K video with cinematic edits, I mean:
> Value
> Clear audio
> No distractions
> Structured video
Consistency of quality tells YouTube that your channel always satisfies its viewers. That gives
YouTube the confidence that you are able to retain people on their platform.
And it goes back to the point I made, YouTube only cares about money so if you can assure
them that you can make them money, they'll continue pushing your channel.
TL;DR: Stop wasting so much time on videos without understanding the core reason why a
video succeeds in the first place. Focus on having a high watch time, a strong idea and
consistently delivering high quality videos.

YouTube External Monetization
Guide by @NotNotAbu2
Chapter 1: Why YouTube AdSense is TERRIBLE
If you’re relying solely on YouTube AdSense to make money, you’re putting your life in someone
else’s hands, someone you don’t even know or trust. YouTube sets the rules, takes the biggest
cut of the pie, and decides how much you earn, all while keeping you on edge with constant
changes to their algorithms and policies. Let’s break down why AdSense isn’t the goldmine it’s
often made out to be.
1. Terrible RPMs
AdSense pays based on RPM, which is the amount you earn per 1,000 views. For most
creators, RPMs are incredibly low. That means even if you’re getting 100,000 views per
video, you might only earn a few hundred dollars. Compare that to the time, effort, and
money you put into creating content, and it quickly becomes clear that AdSense isn’t
lucrative enough.
2. You’re at YouTube’s Mercy
One of the biggest risks of relying on AdSense is that your income can vanish overnight.
YouTube can demonetize your channel for whatever the fuck they decide on that decide.
Videos can be flagged or removed without warning. Algorithm changes can also tank
your views, and there’s nothing you can do about it. Essentially, YouTube holds all the
power, and you’re left scrambling if something goes wrong.
3. High Competition for Views
AdSense revenue is directly tied to views, which means you’re constantly competing for
eyeballs. This pressure often leads creators to chase trends or create clickbait just to
boost their numbers. But even with millions of views, your earnings might still fall short
because the system isn’t built to favor creators, it’s built to favor advertisers.

Chapter 2: External Monetization
External monetization is what ALL of your favorite creators are doing. Even creators you have
never heard of are making millions from YouTube while keeping a low-profile which seems
impossible considering how YouTube works, but it isn't. External monetization is making people
millions, and can make you millions, and you don’t even need to go viral.
But what exactly is external monetization? Simple: making money with products/services.
Yep, nothing revolutionary, but something that most people don’t think about, and something
that most people can’t execute correctly on.
External monetization is always in the back of people’s heads, but 99% of them rather focus on
YouTube’s vanity metrics than make a ton of money and retire their bloodline for good. In this
guide, you will learn everything from A to Z;
a) crucial mindset shifts required to execute on this strategy
b) how to come up with killer products/services to sell
c) how to consistently bring traffic to your marketing videos
d) how to effectively funnel traffic to your product/service
e) how to go about this strategy long-term
Chapter 3: Revenue Streams
This part is SUPER important. Choosing the right product or service will FOREVER dictate how
much money you make, how fast you make it, and how consistently you can make money. It’s
just like ideation with YouTube videos; no matter how good the execution, the video won’t do
well if the idea isn’t strong.
We can divide revenue streams into 3 sections:
1. Physical Product
2. Digital Product
3. Services
1. Physical Products
Very self-explanatory. Physical products are tangible goods that creators sell directly to
their audience. There are 2 famous kinds of physical products:
a) Merchandise
● Mugs
● Clothes
● Tote bags

b) Niche products
● Art supplies
● Fitness gear
● Skincare products
The advantage of physical goods is that it’s really good to build a solid and strong brand.
You build an intimate connection with your audience that will last for a very long time. As
a result, you’ll have a consistent revenue stream and basically anything you do in future
will perform very well.
On the flip side, you’re going to basically be running an e-commerce store, most
probably alone. And e-commerce is very tough and stressful. You not only have to take
care of the product quality, you’ll also have to take care of logistics, supplier
communications, relying on third-party companies (who don’t care about your brand at
all), inventory, complicated maths, and low margins.
Going with physical products as your way to do external monetization isn’t
recommended at all unless you have an established channel and enough resources to
take care of all the headache that comes with selling snacks like MrBeast or drinks like
KSI & Logan Paul.

physical. And it is by far the BEST way to go about external monetization. Digital
products can include:
● Ebooks
● Courses
● Software
● Community
● Exclusive content
etc
Digital Products are objectively the BEST way to do external monetization, doesn’t
matter which level you’re at. You can be a beginner or run an established channel, digital
products will work wonders for you. To begin with, there are VERY LOW overheads, so
you won’t have to worry about logistics, inventory, shipping, supplier communications,
unreliable third-party companies, etc

Chapter 4: Audience’s Importance
Finding your audience and knowing who they are is one of the most critical steps to building a
sustainable and profitable external monetization system. No matter how great your content or
products are, they will only succeed if they connect with the right people. You must know who
you’re selling to, or you’ll end up selling to no one. Do not take this step for granted like 99% of
people do. Through this step, you’ll be able to:
1. Increase engagement
Finding your audience is key to creating content that truly connects with viewers. When
you know your audience, you’re not doing guesswork, you actually tailor your content
specifically to their preferences, problems, and interests. This leads to a deeper
emotional connection. Viewers who feel understood are far more likely to engage with
your videos by liking, commenting, sharing, and watching for longer periods.
For example, if you run a fitness channel and your target audience is busy professionals
who don’t have much time to work out, creating quick 10-minute workouts will resonate
more than generic fitness advice. This alignment between what you create and what
your audience wants results in a community that feels valued, and an audience that is
willing to pay you.

2. Efficient Resource Use
Identifying your target audience saves you time, money, and energy. Without a clear
audience in mind, you’ll be wasting resources and time creating content or products that
won’t give you any returns. For example, you could spend weeks producing a highly
polished video about luxury watches only to realize your audience is more interested in
affordable fashion (because that’s all they can afford).
Knowing your audience allows you to make smarter decisions:
● Content: You’ll avoid trial-and-error guesswork because you know what they
want.
● Product Development: You can design products or services tailored to their
specific needs, increasing the likelihood of success.
Ultimately, this means you’re spending less time and money while achieving better
results. It’s about working smarter, not harder and maximizing the impact of every effort
you put into your channel and business.
3. Long-Term Growth
When you connect deeply with a specific audience, you’re creating a loyal community.
These aren’t just viewers; they’re supporters who trust you, value your
recommendations, and return regularly for your content. Loyal audiences help your
channel grow in several ways:
● Word-of-Mouth Marketing: you’ll grow naturally
● Repeat Customers: you’ll keep making money
[[PAGE 13]]
● Stability: they’ll always be there
By focusing on a specific audience, you create a feedback loop. As you learn more
about them, you can refine your offerings and grow your channel in ways that align with
their needs, ensuring that your success compounds over time.

4. Higher Conversions
When you find your audience, you’re effectively speaking directly to people who are
already interested in what you’re offering. This makes them more likely to take action,
whether it’s subscribing to your channel, buying your product, signing up for your
newsletter, or clicking on an affiliate link.
● Generic Content: You create broad, generalized videos hoping to appeal to
everyone. This may get you to go viral, but if your goal was to go viral, you
wouldn’t be here. Many of these people won’t be interested enough to take
action, and you don’t want that.
● Targeted Content: You focus on a specific group, such as gamers looking for
ergonomic equipment. By showing them products that solve their exact problems,
you’re addressing a need they already have, making it far easier to convert
viewers into customers. You may not go viral, but you’ll make money.
Finding your audience also allows you to focus on quality over quantity. Instead of
chasing views, you’re connecting with the right people who are more likely to spend
money on what you offer. This means higher ROI on your efforts and less dependency
on unpredictable AdSense revenue.

Chapter 6: CCC: Create Content that Converts
Creating content that converts is the secret sauce for turning your YouTube channel into a
money-making machine. If you’ve been reading until here, you’re obviously interested in making
tons of money from YouTube, and simply providing entertainment to your viewers for the sake of
it isn’t your goal. This is where the CCC method comes into place, you satisfy your audience’s
needs and your own goals at the same time.
Let’s break this method down in detail to uncover how you can transform your YouTube content
into a strategic asset for long-term success.
1. Produce the Right Content
The first step in the CCC Method is creating content tailored to the needs, desires, and
challenges of your audience. Your content should provide value, spark interest, and
position you as a credible authority in your niche.
Key Aspects of Effective Content Creation:
● Understand Your Audience - Before creating anything, ensure you have a deep
understanding of who you’re speaking to. What are their pain points? What
problems can you solve for them? Your audience should feel like your videos are
speaking directly to them. If you’re targeting the mass market, your audience
won’t feel like your message is personalized, so you’ll appear as just another
salesman, and thus your conversions will be low.
● Solve Problems - People don’t just watch YouTube for entertainment (a common
misconception everyone has for some reason), they’re also looking for solutions.
51% of people on YouTube are there to learn and educate themselves, that’s
approximately 1,377,000,000 people! Whether it’s “how-to” guides, reviews, or
insights into your niche, offer actionable value that make viewers’ lives easier or
better.

● Focus on Quality Over Quantity - A single well-produced, impactful video can
outperform 10 rushed uploads. Take the time to plan, research, and edit. And I
don’t mean using “Iman Gadzhi” edits or motion graphics for no reason. What I
mean is that you MUST ensure that your video is 10x better than your
competitors in terms of value provided because that is what matters at the end of

A channel focused on fitness might create a video titled “How to Lose Belly Fat in 2
Weeks (Step-by-Step Guide)” This type of content targets a specific problem and
provides value, immediately grabbing the audience’s attention.
2. Align Messaging with Goals
Your content isn’t just about providing value, it’s also about aligning your messaging with
your business goals. To convert viewers into customers, your videos should:
● Introduce Your Offer - Whether you’re selling a product, a digital course, or a
service, subtly mention it into your content. For example, a digital marketing
coach might create videos like “Top 5 Social Media Marketing Tips” while
mentioning their coaching program as a resource to learn more.
● Build Trust and Credibility - People only buy from creators they trust. Share
your expertise, provide social proof (like testimonials or results), and show
authenticity in your delivery. The more credible you appear, the more willing
viewers will be to take action.
● Use Clear Calls-to-Action (CTAs) - Your CTAs should be specific and
actionable. Instead of vague phrases like “Check it out,” use clear instructions
like “Click the link in the description to download your free guide” or “Sign up for
my course today.”. Just don’t appear too salesy.

3. Optimize For Watch Time
Your content needs to keep people watching. The longer someone stays on your video,
the more the YouTube algorithm rewards you. But beyond algorithm favor, it also means

[[PAGE 17]]

4. Build A Library
You want a backlog of videos that compound in views and conversions over time. A
complete video library targets each stage of the buyer journey. Think in terms of:
● Awareness videos - mass appeal, to generate leads
● Problem videos - pain-focused, to nurture your leads
● Solution videos - offer-focused, to get more conversions
Over time, your channel becomes a living portfolio. One video may act as the entry point,
another educates, and another closes the sale. This ecosystem works 24/7. If all your
videos are awareness videos, viewers may never move to action. If all are pitch-heavy,
you won’t get new viewers. Build your library like a sales funnel.

Chapter 7: Overcoming Challenges
On a realistic note, external monetization isn’t as easy as posting a few videos and watching
money pour in. Most people fail because they hit these challenges and never recover. Here’s
how to handle them.
1. Low Views
This is the #1 killer of motivation. But here’s the truth: views don’t matter if you’re
monetizing correctly. A channel with 1,000 views per video can outperform a viral
channel with no monetization strategy. However, this problem is very nuanced because
you do not need tons of views to make external monetization work, and your views are
dependent on the category of video you are making. So you can have less views, but a
lot more conversions with a bottom-of-the-funnel video.
Fix:
● Integrate current issues/trends into your video idea.
● Focus on solving problems that your audience actively searches for.
2. Impostor Syndrome
If you are starting out with a new product, you’ll feel like you’re not good enough to sell
something. You’ll ask, “Why would anyone buy from me?”. Don’t worry, this is a feeling
many people have. But as long as you’re confident about your product and the value
you’re able to provide, external monetization won’t be an issue.
Fix:
● Start small, sell a low-ticket product and get feedback.
[[PAGE 18]]
● Share your journey transparently, do not pressurize yourself to be the best.
3. Overwhelmed
There are tons of things you have to learn when starting with external monetization.
Funnels, email lists, landing pages, payment processors, it can all feel overwhelming.
Fix:
● Start with one simple offer and one landing page.
● Focus on revenue first, worry about optimization later.
● Consult with an expert (you can book a call with me)

4. Fear of Selling
People don’t want to be “salesy” or pushy (obviously). But this is the wrong mindset that

you view yourself as “salesy”, your viewers don’t.

● Change your mindset. You’re not selling, you’re offering a solution to their pain.
● Reframe your CTA to appear as if you’re doing a favour to viewers.

Youtube virality external monetization guide
YouTube is unfair.
Some channels go viral overnight, others grind for years and still get nowhere.
[[PAGE 19]]
From day one, you are put up against creators who have:
> Momentum
> Bigger budgets
> More experience
> Better storytelling
> Established audience
That means you are losing the game from the very start.
This is because YouTube's goal is to keep viewers watching ads, not to help creators.
And for YouTube to achieve their goal, they have to play favorites. Not necessarily based on
who you are, but on who can prove they’ll deliver right now.
A brand-new creator can blow up overnight if their first video crushes the competition's video.
Whereas a 10-year "veteran" will always be ignored if their videos just don't match up to the
competition.
That’s why growth compounds for those who go viral. Once YouTube sees your videos
consistently perform above average, it starts testing them with bigger audiences faster. Even
your future uploads get more impressions before they’ve even proven themselves because of
the channel's track record.
Unfortunately, YouTube doesn't really give you a 2nd chance.
Made by NotNotAbu2
Made by NotNotAbu2
If you upload a streak of weak videos early on, the algorithm has no reason to trust your future
uploads, because the data keeps saying over and over again that people don't like this channel.
Reversing that is possible, but it takes time, consistency, and better execution.
Many creators hate hearing this because it feels unfair - rightfully so.
And it is unfair if you’re expecting YouTube to treat everyone equally, but it doesn't. It’s a
ruthless meritocracy where every upload is a high-stakes performance review.
But here's how you can fix it:
Step 1: Accept the unfairness
Stop expecting the algorithm to give you a chance just because. YouTube is a data-driven
machine that rewards proven performance.
Every recommendation your video gets is a risk for YouTube. If it underperforms, that’s not just
bad for you, it’s also bad for YouTube’s business because a viewer could click away, lowering
their ad revenue.
This is why YouTube is super strict and doesn't give your video unlimited impressions unless it
deserves it. They have no reason to gamble on you unless you’ve shown, through consistent
results, that you can keep people watching longer than the competition.
Dropping the “fairness” mindset is step one, because it changes you into a ruthless competitor.
Step 2: Reverse-engineer what’s already winning
Your niche probably has a handful of videos that are dominating right now. YouTube is feeding
these videos to viewers because they’ve proven, with hard numbers, that they can keep
attention.
Now your job is to break those videos down:
> What colors, compositions, and emotions are they using in the thumbnail?
> What title formats are they using? How do the titles spark curiosity or create urgency?
> How often do the visuals change? How quickly do they get to the point?
> What's the pay-off of these videos? What value are they giving to the audience?
Made by NotNotAbu2
Made by NotNotAbu2
[[PAGE 20]]
Step 3: Publish only videos you know will outperform
Before uploading, look at the top video your target viewer is currently seeing. Then ask yourself:
“If I was scrolling through YouTube, would I click my video or the competitor's?” If your honest
answer is “probably not,” that’s a red flag.
Being ruthless at this stage is essential. This means even abandoning decent ideas that aren’t
strong enough, reworking concepts until the title and thumbnail are irresistible, and refusing to
upload until you’ve built something that’s a banger.
Also make sure every single aspect of your video is backed by data. If you're using a certain
word in the title, there must be data saying that using that word will positively affect the video.
TL;DR: YouTube rewards proven performance. Some creators blow up because they outperform
competition from day one, while some can't seem to blow up after years of making videos.
Accept the unfairness, study what’s winning, and stack consistent outperformance until the
algorithm trusts you.
Perfect — this is a massive update video that redefines how the YouTube algorithm works in

Here’s a detailed breakdown of what the speakers (Rene Ritchie + Todd Beaupré) are actually saying,
🧠 PART 1: What Todd & Rene Are Saying (in simple terms)
what it means strategically, and what I’d recommend you do next as a creator or strategist.
1. The Algorithm Doesn’t “Push” Videos — It “Pulls” for Each Viewer
“It isn’t about pushing videos out. It’s about pulling the best content for each individual viewer.”
 ●​ YouTube no longer looks at your video and decides who to show it to.
 ●​ Instead, it looks at the viewer and decides what videos might make them happiest today.
 ●​ It’s not video-centric anymore. It’s viewer-centric.
Key meaning:​
Every viewer’s homepage is custom-built. It’s not about your video fighting for global reach — it’s
about whether your video fits the viewer’s identity cluster (based on interest patterns, habits, device,
and satisfaction history).
2. YouTube “Automates Word of Mouth”
“We describe recommendations as automating word of mouth.”
 ●​ The system learns what other viewers like you are watching.
 ●​ It copies the “friend recommendation” model.
 ●​ That’s why “clusters” (communities of similar viewers) are so important — if your video clicks
 with one cluster, it can snowball organically.
Key meaning:​
Audience discovery = finding your cluster. The algorithm isn’t random; it’s looking for viewer tribes
who behave alike.
3. The Algorithm Recycles Old Videos
“A video can find new audiences months or years later.”
 ●​ YouTube keeps resurfacing videos when new events, trends, or nostalgic spikes make them
 relevant again.
 ●​ You don’t lose relevance — videos can “rebloom” with new context.
[[PAGE 21]]
Key meaning:​
YouTube is more like Netflix than TikTok — videos have long-tail life if the topic regains cultural heat.
4. Context-Aware Recommendations (Device, Time, Mood)
“You might see different results on your TV at night vs. your phone in the morning.”
 ●​ YouTube now uses contextual signals (device, time, viewing mood).
 ●​ Example: news in the morning, comedy at night.
Key meaning:​
If you post certain content types, time of publishing and first-hour engagement matter more —
because the system tests different contexts to learn your ideal window.
5. No Single “Success Metric” (CTR ≠ Everything)
“There’s no single number. Watch time, CTR, likes — all vary in importance depending on content
type and context.”
 ●​ YouTube doesn’t rank purely by CTR or watch time.
 ●​ For music, likes may matter more than duration.
 ●​ For podcasts, session time or completion rate may matter more.
Key meaning:​
Optimize your metric based on format intent. Example:
 ●​ Educational videos → retention curve.
 ●​ Emotional storytelling → satisfaction + likes.
 ●​ Binge series → multi-video sessions (end screens).
6. YouTube Optimizes for Viewer Satisfaction, Not Just Watch Time
“We’ve learned not all time spent is equally valuable.”
 ●​ They now use surveys, likes, dislikes, and “Not Interested” to measure how satisfied people
 feel.
 ●​ “Satisfaction” feeds directly into ranking.
 ●​ Long-term retention (returning to YouTube) matters more than short-term watch time.
Key meaning:​
Clickbait that doesn’t fulfill its promise gets punished.​
Creators who deliver emotional or informational payoff per minute are rewarded.
7. Focus on Long-Term Viewer Relationship
“We want viewers to keep coming back because we deliver value in the long run.”
 ●​ YouTube’s goal aligns with creator goals — keep viewers returning.
 ●​ Channels that consistently satisfy specific clusters get more “future impressions.”
Key meaning:​
Don’t chase one viral — chase trust signals over multiple uploads. The system promotes predictability
and relationship-building.
8. Benchmarks Are Useless Across Channels
“Your CTR and watch time aren’t comparable across other creators.”
 ●​ CTR, AVD, or retention can’t be compared across niches.
 ●​ Even within your own channel, context (topic appeal, timing) shifts metrics.
[[PAGE 22]]
Key meaning:​
Compare your videos only within your audience cluster.​
The goal isn’t high CTR; it’s relative CTR vs similar videos YouTube could’ve shown instead.
9. Multi-Language Support Is Now Algorithmic
“We added feedback loops per language. Aim for 80% catalog coverage per language.”
 ●​ Multi-audio dubs are now fully algorithm-aware.
 ●​ YouTube separately tracks performance per dub.
 ●​ Channels dubbing at least 80% of catalog in key languages perform better.
Key meaning:​
YouTube is global-first now. Multi-language dubs aren’t optional; they’re a growth accelerator.
10. View Dips Are Normal — It’s Supply & Demand
“Interest waves and content supply affect your view dips.”
 ●​ Your views going down doesn’t mean your channel is dying.
 ●​ Trends saturate: high demand early → low supply → high views.​
 Later → high supply → fewer views per creator.
Key meaning:​
Ride new demand waves before they saturate. Use Google Trends + audience data to pivot early.
11. Use the Subscriptions Tab as a Pure Signal
“It’s the only feed not influenced by the algorithm.”
 ●​ Subscription feed = clean testing ground.
 ●​ It helps you test if core audience still clicks and retains.
Key meaning:​
If your subscribers stop clicking in Sub Tab → problem is topic or thumbnail, not algorithm.
12. Large Language Models Now Power Recommendations
“We’re using LLMs to better understand nuance, tone, and intent.”
 ●​ YouTube now uses AI similar to ChatGPT to:
 ●​ Understand content style, emotion, context, ingredients of topics.
 ●​ Match videos to viewers on deeper psychological levels.
Key meaning:​
Algorithm isn’t just “data-driven” — it’s semantic + emotional.​
Thumbnails, tone, story style, and topic framing matter even more — because AI understands human

Excellent — this is one of the most valuable algorithm breakdowns I’ve seen lately because it bridges
storytelling, psychology, and algorithmic logic. Let’s go layer-by-layer through what the creator is really
[[PAGE 24]]
saying about the YouTube algorithm, what we can learn from it, and my professional suggestions for
🧠 What the Person is Saying About the YouTube Algorithm
applying it in 2025’s landscape.
1️⃣ The Algorithm Doesn’t “Favor” You — It Favors Viewer Response
 ●​ The creator debunks the myth that the algorithm “rewards” consistency or effort.
 ●​ YouTube’s system only cares about one thing: time watched + satisfaction loops (shares,
 likes, replays, comments).
 ●​ The only way to activate the algorithm is to trigger strong emotional transfer that makes
 viewers discuss or rewatch.
👉 Core takeaway: YouTube doesn’t “push” creators. It amplifies content that keeps people engaged
— emotionally and socially.
2️⃣ Emotional Transfer = Algorithm Fuel
 ●​ The speaker says the #1 predictor of performance is emotional transfer — how strongly your
 video makes someone feel something.
 ●​ Emotions like awe, shock, fear, inspiration, curiosity spark higher retention, more
 comments, and sharing.
 ●​ Algorithms detect these indirectly through viewer behaviors (watch time, replay rate,
 comments, shares).
👉 Emotional resonance → conversation → sharing → algorithmic growth.​
This mirrors the “commentary value score (CVS)” framework: a video that generates arguments or
excitement performs better.
3️⃣ “Speed to Value” Is the Hidden Retention Metric
 ●​ Most creators overload the viewer with info. That causes drop-offs, even if the info is great.
 ●​ The algorithm interprets early exits as disinterest.
 ●​ You should aim to deliver a dopamine hit of value (insight, surprise, or payoff) in the first
 7–10 seconds for Shorts or first 45–60 seconds for longform.
👉 Think of this like retention physics:
Shorter “time to dopamine” = higher retention curve = stronger viewer satisfaction signal =
more impressions.
4️⃣ Algorithm Myths Are Killing Growth
 ●​ Creators blame “shadowbans” or “YouTube hates small channels,” but it’s not personal.
 ●​ When your video doesn’t get impressions, it’s not being suppressed — it’s just not generating
 strong enough viewer data in the early test groups.
 ●​ The system tests every video with a small cluster. If that cluster doesn’t respond, it dies early.
 ●​ So, quality and resonance per viewer in those first clusters matter more than frequency.
5️⃣ The Algorithm Is Emotionally Binary
It’s either:
“This video triggered engagement — expand it,”​
or​
“This video was ignored — stop showing it.”
There’s no middle ground. Every decision the system makes comes from that early audience test.
[[PAGE 25]]
6️⃣ The “Content Legos” Framework = Scientific Iteration
 ●​ Every video is made of nine algorithmic levers (topic, angle, hook, storytelling, visuals,
 audio, title, thumbnail, pacing).
 ●​ Instead of changing everything at once, isolate one Lego and improve it.
 ●​ This is how big creators find “what actually matters” instead of guessing.
 ●​ The algorithm rewards consistency of viewer satisfaction, not randomness.
👉 When one Lego improves watch time or CTR, keep it — that becomes part of your signature
pattern YouTube starts associating with your channel.
7️⃣ The Algorithm Now Rewards “Newness” Over “Follower Count”
 ●​ Since 2022, recommendation systems don’t depend on subscriber history anymore.
 ●​ Meaning: any video can go viral, even from a 0-subscriber channel — if it triggers strong
 metrics.
 ●​ The algorithm ranks videos by viewer match, not creator history.
👉 Translation: every upload is a fresh audition to YouTube’s viewer clusters.
💡 What I Understand From This Video
This creator is reframing the YouTube algorithm not as a technical system but as a psychological
mirror of audience reaction.​
It’s not about:
 ●​ SEO
 ●​ tags
 ●​ upload time
 ●​ or posting consistency
It’s about:
“How fast and how deeply can you make someone feel something worth discussing?”
🚀 My Suggestions Based on This Framework
So, the algorithm is basically an emotion detector disguised as math.
1️⃣ Design for “Speed to Emotion”
 ●​ Don’t open with context — open with an emotional hook.
 ●​ Example: Instead of​
 “Today we’re talking about how AI is changing education.”​
 Say:​
 “In the next 10 years, kids might not learn how to think — and AI could be the reason.”
→ 3-second curiosity. Immediate stakes.
2️⃣ Write Scripts Around “Emotional Charge”
 ●​ Before finalizing a script, ask:​
 “What 3 comments will my superfan, neutral, and hater each leave?”
 ●​ If you can’t imagine all three, your video lacks tension.
 ●​ The best-performing videos are those that polarize slightly — they don’t leave everyone
 lukewarm.
[[PAGE 26]]
3️⃣ Build Your Channel Like a Scientist (Content Legos)
 ●​ Treat each upload as a controlled experiment: change one variable only.
 ●​ Track CTR, average view duration, and AVD/CTR correlation per Lego change.
 ●​ Over 10–15 uploads, you’ll identify your conversion Legos (formats that yield consistent
 watch-time growth).
4️⃣ Stop “Over-educating” in One Video
 ●​ Focus on one big idea per video, not 10 small ones.
 ●​ YouTube’s algorithm rewards clarity of value, not density of information.
 ●​ Each video should feel like one completed thought — not a lecture.
5️⃣ Engineer for Comment Density
 ●​ End every video on a provocation, not a conclusion.​
 Example:​
 “If AI raises our kids better than we do… do we even deserve to be parents?”
 ●​ This fuels comments, argument threads, and engagement loops.
6️⃣ Approach Ideation as “Remix Culture”
 ●​ Don’t chase originality. Chase pattern remixing.
 ●​ Find top-performing ideas in your niche, change angle or context by 3–20%, and retell it in
 your voice.
 ●​ Algorithms reward familiar novelty — recognizable structure, fresh execution.
7️⃣ Optimize for Cluster Growth, Not Channel Growth
 ●​ The “audience discovery” phase is YouTube’s way of testing you with micro-clusters.
 ●​ Your first 3–5 uploads must clearly target the same emotional + demographic audience.
 ●​ That helps YouTube map your “ideal viewer” and grow you faster.
⚙️ Final Synthesis: The 2025 YouTube Algorithm in One Line
YouTube doesn’t reward creators — it rewards emotional consistency that leads to repeat
viewing within the same cluster of humans.
If you can engineer for that, you’re not fighting the algorithm — you’re speaking its language.

🧠 Part 1 — What the Creator Is Saying About the YouTube Algorithm
Let’s break it down clearly into two parts:
1. Algorithm = Audience
“एल्गोरिदम इज इक्वल टू ऑडियंस” (The algorithm is the audience)
This is the core truth:​
YouTube’s algorithm doesn’t decide what to promote on its own — it reacts to what viewers do.​
It studies how real humans:
 ●​ Click (CTR)
 ●​ Watch (Retention)
 ●​ Rewatch, share, or leave (Satisfaction)
So the algorithm = a mirror of audience behavior.​
If the audience likes something → algorithm pushes it to more similar people.​
If they ignore or skip → it stops pushing.
He’s saying:
“You can’t please the algorithm directly; you please the audience, and the algorithm follows.”
2. Two Sources of Data: Creator + Viewer
The algorithm collects signals from two sides:
 Source What It Learns
Creator-sid Video language, location, metadata, title, tags, audience age range, etc.
e
[[PAGE 32]]
Viewer-side What they click, how long they watch, what they skip, what they
 rewatch.
So YouTube matches the right videos to the right viewers using this combined data.​
This is what YouTube calls “audience-video matching.”
3. YouTube Judges Data, Not Quality
“एल्गोरिथम तुम्हारा वीडियो नहीं बल्कि डाटा दे खता है”​
(“The algorithm doesn’t see your video — it sees your data.”)
A brilliant line.​
YouTube doesn’t “watch” your video — it only sees:
 ●​ Click-through rate (CTR)
 ●​ Average view duration
 ●​ Audience retention curve
 ●​ Satisfaction metrics (likes, comments, “not interested” signals)
No matter how beautiful or cinematic your video is, if viewers don’t click or don’t watch long
enough, the system assumes it’s not satisfying.
4. The Two “Magical” Metrics — CTR and AR
He calls them the two magical topics:
 ●​ CTR (Click-Through Rate): How many people clicked your video out of total impressions.
 ●​ Higher CTR = stronger first impression.
 ●​ Influenced mainly by title + thumbnail.
 ●​ AR (Audience Retention): How long people keep watching your video.
 ●​ Higher retention = stronger proof of viewer satisfaction.
 ●​ Influenced by pacing, storytelling, editing.
He explains them with math examples (like 55 views from 1100 impressions = 5% CTR).​
That’s how YouTube quantifies initial click attraction and ongoing engagement.
5. The Ideal Thresholds
He suggests:
 ●​ CTR > 7% → strong chance to go viral
 ●​ Retention > 40% for short videos (under 10 mins)
 ●​ Retention > 30% for long videos (15–20 mins)
These are indeed reasonable targets in modern YouTube analytics.​
Videos hitting these numbers often trigger recommendation expansion.
6. The Real Secret — The Video Idea
“CTR और AR जरूरी हैं, लेकिन उससे भी ज्यादा जरूरी है वीडियो आइडिया।”
This is the most important takeaway.​
He’s saying:
 ●​ Metrics help only if the core idea is strong.
 ●​ A boring topic with great editing won’t perform.
 ●​ A powerful, curiosity-driven, emotionally sticky idea can go viral even with weak SEO or
 average production.

 ●​ YouTube doesn’t randomly “blast” your video to people.
 ●​ Instead, it watches what viewers are already watching, and then tries to find more videos like
 those to recommend next.

loop.​
If not → it sits invisible.

He says:

specific viewer’s interests.

⚙️ PART 2 — What I understand from this (the deeper
meaning)
🔹 1. YouTube is an Audience Simulator
This video essentially reframes how creators should think about YouTube in 2025:
 ●​ It’s like a massive social lab running millions of micro-experiments.
 ●​ Each video impression is a test: “If I show this to this type of viewer, how do they respond?”
 ●​ The algorithm keeps refining its matches based on these responses.​
 → So creators are not fighting the algorithm — they’re feeding it training data through their
 audience’s behavior.
🔹 2. Discovery is Cluster-Based, Not Channel-Based
 ●​ YouTube doesn’t care about your subscriber count; it cares about viewer clusters.
 ●​ When your video performs well within one cluster (say, “space enthusiasts” or “DIY home
 repair fans”), the system will amplify it to similar clusters.​
 → This is why one viral hit can pull a whole channel upward if all your videos fit that same
 audience DNA.
🔹 3. CTR + Retention + Satisfaction = Algorithmic Trust Loop
[[PAGE 40]]
 ●​ CTR (click temptation) tells YouTube: “Viewers are curious.”
 ●​ Retention tells it: “Viewers are satisfied.”
 ●​ Repeat viewing tells it: “This creator is reliable.”​
 → When these three signals align, YouTube expands your reach exponentially because your
 video is now predictably enjoyable to a certain type of viewer.
🔹 4. The Algorithm is Emotionally Intelligent (Sort of)
The 2025 system focuses more on satisfaction signals (like likes, replays, watch streaks, and
survey responses) — meaning it’s learning what feels good to people, not just what they click.
🔹 5. YouTube rewards “watching ecosystems,” not individual uploads
So creators win by making content that sustains emotional interest, not just intellectual interest.
If your videos connect together (same tone, style, viewer persona), viewers chain-watch your content
→ YouTube reads this as high satisfaction → and expands your distribution.​
✅
This ties back to your earlier 3-video launch idea — it’s a mini “ecosystem test.”
 In short:​
The YouTube algorithm in 2025 is less of a “gatekeeper” and more of a dynamic matchmaker AI that
continuously learns which videos create emotional satisfaction and viewing loops for specific audience
clusters.

⚙️ The Underlying System (Decoded)
If we convert his philosophy into algorithm logic:
 1.​ Data Collection Layer (Discovery Test)
 ●​ YouTube shows your video to a small group (impression burst).
 ●​ Measures: CTR, AVD (Average View Duration), retention curve.
 2.​ Confidence Threshold
 ●​ If early metrics exceed baseline → expands test.
 ●​ If not → video dies out (flatline).
 3.​ Audience Profiling
 ●​ Each interaction trains a “viewer fingerprint” for your channel.
 ●​ High topical consistency = faster audience clustering.
 4.​ Recommendation Acceleration
 ●​ Once YouTube knows your audience type (e.g. “DIY furniture enthusiasts”), it
 recommends your future uploads faster.
So his “4 signals” strategy = artificially speeding up that feedback loop by:
 ●​ Using search (clear intent signal)
 ●​ Using consistent topic (clear viewer type)
 ●​ Using volume (more data points)
 ●​ Using thumbnails that drive CTR (cleaner testing data)

🧠 B. Comment Replies = Hidden Retention Signal
YouTube’s AI now trusts behavioral proof over channel history.
When he says “reply to every comment,” he’s describing a social feedback loop:
 ●​ A viewer comments → creator replies → viewer gets notified → they return to the video.​
 This inflates session time and return view rate — both indirectly tell the algorithm:
“This creator keeps people in the ecosystem.”​
Hence, YouTube rewards that video/channel.
🧠 C. Posting Time = Acceleration Trigger, Not Visibility Cause
So this isn’t a soft tactic — it’s behavioral reactivation engineering.

lot.​
If you post when your audience is awake and active → more watch data → more positive signals →
faster recommendation ramp-up.
🧠 D. Title–Tag–Script Alignment = Metadata Integrity
So the algorithm doesn’t care what time, it cares who’s available to prove your content is good.
YouTube’s AI models (especially DeepMind + MUM) analyze language and semantics.​

“This video delivers what it promises.”​
That improves recommendation precision — YouTube knows who to serve it to.
He’s right — misalignment looks like clickbait → high CTR but low satisfaction → algorithm throttles

reach.

 ●​ Semantic clarity (aligned metadata)
 ●​ Temporal optimization (first 6 hours’ performance)
 ●​ Emotional reciprocity (viewers feeling connected)

[[PAGE 48]]
 1.​ Intent & Context over Metadata
 ●​ The algorithm no longer just reads tags and titles; it interprets viewer intent through
 captions, watch behavior, and topic clusters.
 ●​ That’s why your first 15 seconds, title wording, and description tone matter more
 than pure keywords.

 ●​ The thumbnail/title combo forms your first algorithmic signal.

 time, a top-ranking factor.
 3.​ AI-assisted Upload & Discovery
 ●​ YouTube is now integrating multi-thumbnail testing, AI categorization, and
 synthetic content labeling, which means the system learns more from creator
 behavior.
 ●​ Clean metadata (titles/descriptions/tags) trains YouTube’s AI model for better
 contextual pairing.
 4.​ Human Clarity = Algorithm Confidence
 ●​ The more structured and transparent your upload info (description, labels,
 disclosure), the more confidence signals YouTube assigns to your content.
 ●​ This improves your Recommendation Probability Score (RPS) behind the scenes.

This creator’s insights confirm several deep truths about YouTube’s internal logic:
 1.​ YouTube’s first priority is viewer satisfaction, not creator consistency.​
 If a viewer watches two of your videos → algorithm reads that as a “pattern of satisfaction”.
 2.​ Shorts are tested fast and shallow (small clusters first).​
 The first hour determines if your video deserves wider exposure. This is why timing +
 engagement velocity matter most.
 3.​ Browse and Shorts feeds use slightly different algorithms.
 ●​ Shorts Feed: Prioritizes watch duration, swipe speed, replays.
 ●​ Browse Feed: Prioritizes CTR (click-through rate) and watch time.​
 → By adding thumbnails, you’re tapping into both systems.
 4.​ Behavioral data > Metadata.​
 YouTube uses AI video analysis, sound recognition, and text overlays to understand topics
 better than hashtags or keywords.
 5.​ Uploading method and early watch velocity matter more than tags or SEO.​
 The platform is behavioral, not descriptive.
 6.​ Multi-video watch sessions signal trust.​
 This links perfectly with your earlier quote — multiple videos viewed by one person = stronger
 “cluster confidence” = faster channel growth.

⚙️ WHAT THIS REALLY MEANS (Algorithm Understanding)

YouTube uses multi-stage learning for recommendations:
 1.​ Cold Start Stage (Metadata)​
 → YouTube relies heavily on text data: titles, tags, and descriptions.​
 → The algorithm clusters your videos with similar content types.
[[PAGE 61]]
 2.​ Testing Stage (Viewer Behavior)​
 → It shows your video to small batches of users in similar interest clusters.​
 → If CTR (click-through rate) + AVD (average view duration) are good, it expands testing.
 3.​ Scaling Stage (Recommendation)​
 → Videos start appearing in “Suggested,” “Browse,” and “Home.”​
 → Metadata becomes less important — viewer satisfaction signals take over.
So what this creator is showing is the Stage 1 “bootstrapping” technique — helping the algorithm

guess your niche faster through metadata optimization.

🎯 What the Person Is Saying About the YouTube Algorithm
Let’s break it down deeply
The creator is explaining a common but critical mistake new YouTubers make — publishing their
videos immediately after uploading.
He says:
“Most new creators directly hit ‘Public’ after upload, and then wonder why views don’t come.”
Then he reveals the actual reason — not editing, not thumbnail, not content — but a timing
🔍 Core Explanation of How the Algorithm Works (as per the video)
problem in how YouTube’s algorithm processes new uploads.
 1.​ YouTube first “tests” every new video.​
 When you publish, YouTube shows your video to a small test audience (usually viewers
 similar to your subscribers or those who watched related content).
 2.​ If the test audience ignores it or clicks away early,​
 YouTube assumes your video isn’t satisfying and stops recommending it further.
 3.​ The reason for low performance:​
 When you publish instantly after upload, YouTube’s systems don’t get enough time to:
 ●​ Analyze your title & keywords
 ●​ Understand your thumbnail visually
 ●​ Scan your description & tags
 ●​ Match your video to the right audience cluster
 4.​ So, YouTube shows it to the wrong people → low CTR & watch time → negative signals →
 the video “dies early.”
⚙️ The Creator’s Recommended Solution: “Scheduling”
He says the best practice is to always schedule your videos instead of publishing immediately.
Why?
Because:
 ●​ When you schedule a video (even for the next day),
 ●​ YouTube gets a few hours to process and categorize it.
 ●​ The algorithm learns which audience might be ideal.
 ●​ So, when the video goes live, it’s already pre-matched to the right viewers.
 ●​ Result → higher CTR, better retention, more consistent views.
He even says:
“हर बड़ा यूट्यूबर अपनी वीडियो को कभी डायरेक्ट पब्लिक नहीं करता — हम शेड्यूल करते हैं।”
🧩 Additional Tips He Shares
(Every big YouTuber never goes directly public — we schedule.)
 1.​ Upload from Chrome desktop, not the mobile app.​
 Because sometimes the mobile app fails to send “notify subscribers” signals.
 2.​ Schedule for 24–48 hours later.​
 Gives the algorithm full time to prepare & categorize.
 3.​ Best times to publish:
[[PAGE 63]]
 ●​ Morning: 7–9 AM
 ●​ Evening: 5–8 PM (when audience activity peaks)
 4.​ Don’t overuse Premieres.
 ●​ Premieres are good only for special launches (music videos, films, trailers).
 ●​ For daily content, it actually hurts because YouTube doesn’t get enough time to
 pre-process or find the right audience.
🧠 What I Understand from This Video
This video is not really about “hacking” the algorithm — it’s about understanding the pre-launch
mechanics of YouTube’s recommendation system.
When a video is uploaded, YouTube uses machine learning to:
 ●​ Extract metadata from title/description/tags.
 ●​ Visually analyze the thumbnail and video frames.
 ●​ Match all of that with potential “viewer clusters” (people who might click/watch).
If you publish instantly, you cut that preparation window short — and YouTube is “forced” to test
your video on random people. That damages your initial impression click-through rate, and the
algorithm deprioritizes you early.
💡 My Suggestions (Strategic + Algorithmic)
So, scheduling is a smart “pre-launch optimization” tactic.
✅ 1. Treat Uploading Like a Launch, Not a Drop
Don’t just hit publish. Give YouTube 12–24 hours to “read” your content metadata.​
✅ 2. Always Schedule Uploads
Think of it like giving Google SEO time to crawl a webpage before indexing it.
Even scheduling for next morning can make a difference — especially for small/new channels.​
✅ 3. Optimize Metadata Before Scheduling
This is the “algorithm warm-up” stage where YouTube categorizes your video properly.
Make sure:
 ●​ Title has clear intent & keywords.
 ●​ Thumbnail matches the emotion and context.
 ●​ Description has strong first 2 lines for SEO.
 ●​ Tags match your niche’s search behavior.
✅ 4. Don’t Use Premieres Unless It’s an Event
This gives the algorithm strong initial context before it tests your video.
Premieres delay processing and confuse the algorithm about the video’s “event nature.”​
✅ 5. Maintain Upload Consistency
Use it only for big releases or fan-engagement events — not for tutorials or daily uploads.
Scheduling helps you:
 ●​ Batch record & upload.
 ●​ Stay consistent (YouTube loves predictability).
 ●​ Give the algorithm time to pattern-match your content with ideal viewer clusters.

🧠 What the Creator is Actually Saying (Core Message
Let’s break it down into three layers:
Summary)
1. The Algorithm Has Evolved
 ●​ YouTube is no longer search-based (what people type in) but recommendation-based (what
 people should see).
 ●​ When a new channel uploads, YouTube first tests their videos with a small sample of
 viewers.
 ●​ Based on engagement, it decides whether to push further.
 ●​ This causes early ups and downs — initial small reach, a sudden boost, then flat growth.
 ●​ Creators misinterpret this dip, panic, and switch topics too soon — which resets the
 algorithm’s learning again and again.
🔹 Lesson: YouTube tests you. Don’t confuse “no growth” with “no potential.” Stay the course.
2. YouTube Pushes Focused, Consistent Channels
[[PAGE 67]]
 ●​ YouTube’s system builds “viewer clusters” for each channel.
 ●​ If your topics are random (one vlog, one gaming, one education), the algorithm can’t define
 your audience.
 ●​ Hence, no consistent momentum.
 ●​ You must maintain “value consistency” — not just upload frequency.
🔹 Lesson: Keep your core audience promise fixed. You can change subtopics, but not your mission.
3. Retention Is the Real Algorithm
 ●​ YouTube doesn’t reward hard work or knowledge.
 ●​ It rewards attention.
 ●​ Retention flow = Thumbnail → Title → Hook → Continuous micro-rewards (every few
 seconds).
 ●​ If your thumbnail doesn’t stop scrolling, if the hook doesn’t fulfill the title’s promise, you lose
 the viewer instantly.
🔹 Lesson: YouTube is not a “video” platform — it’s an attention platform.
4. Understand the “Valley of Death”
 ●​ Even when you fix retention and consistency, there’s a long period (weeks or months) where
 you’ll get little to no growth.
 ●​ This is when YouTube is still testing your audience.
 ●​ Most small creators quit here, mistaking testing for failure.
🔹 Lesson: Survive the Valley of Death by focusing on research + execution, not analytics obsession.
5. The Growth Roadmap (10 → 100K Framework)
 Phase Focus Key Action
1. Focus Data Give YouTube clear signals Stick to one sub-niche (e.g., “Desk
 about your niche Workouts” not “Fitness”)
2. Content Validation Test variations within that Post 10–15 videos with different angles;
 sub-niche double down on what performs
3. Retention Flow Optimize viewer experience Improve hook, pacing, reward moments
4. Valley of Death Survive the dry phase Keep posting + study competitors
5. Expansion Phase Broaden niche gradually Go from sub-niche → niche → wider
(after 5K subs) audience
🚀 What I Understand from It (Algorithm Logic)
6. Sustain Momentum Systematize creation Build repeatable content systems
The creator is describing YouTube’s Machine Learning feedback loop in simple language:
 1.​ YouTube tests your videos → 1000 viewers → measures watch time, CTR, retention.
 2.​ If audience engagement > benchmark, it increases exposure.
 3.​ If you change content direction, YouTube loses its data model on your channel → resets
 your progress.
 4.​ Algorithm = human behavior learning model → It learns who likes your videos only when
 you stay predictable.
💡 My Professional Suggestions for Creators
So, growth = train the algorithm by training your content signals.
1. Build “Signal Clarity”
[[PAGE 68]]
 ●​ Use one color palette, tone, and thumbnail style so YouTube can visually cluster your
 channel.
 ●​ Keep metadata consistent: title style, keywords, niche tags.
 ●​ Example: If you’re “Desk Fitness Guy,” every upload should scream that visually and
 contextually.
2. Master the Retention Loop
Every second must “pay off” the viewer’s curiosity.​
Use this 4-layer retention model:
 Layer Viewer Emotion Tool

sec

3. Use A/B Testing Aggressively
 ●​ Upload same video with two thumbnails (via YouTube Experiment feature).
 ●​ Use “CTR + Avg View Duration” matrix to judge thumbnail quality.
 ●​ If CTR < 5% → fix title/thumbnail.
 ●​ If AVD < 40% → fix pacing/hook.
4. Don’t Chase Virality, Chase Data Density
 ●​ 15 focused videos in one sub-niche give YouTube clean data → the algorithm can model
 audience intent.
 ●​ Random videos confuse the model → no reach.
 ●​ Treat your first 50 videos as “machine training data.”
5. Adopt a Long-Term Mindset
“Your first 100 videos teach YouTube who you are.​
Your next 100 teach YouTube who loves you.”

He’s essentially describing the YouTube algorithm’s trust-building and audience testing cycle.
When a video goes live:
 1.​ YouTube doesn’t promote it broadly.
 2.​ It tests it with a small sample.
 3.​ The data from those first 50–500 viewers decides whether it deserves further distribution.
So if you ruin that data (e.g. send irrelevant WhatsApp traffic, have no comments, or get bad retention
early), the algorithm concludes your video doesn’t satisfy users — even if it’s actually good.
He’s teaching creators how to optimize that testing phase manually:
 ●​ Give it clean engagement signals.
 ●​ Don’t pollute it with wrong traffic.
 ●​ Stimulate engagement (comments + replies).
 ●​ Use internal YouTube tools (community tab, analytics) instead of external spam.

🧠 2. What This Really Means / What I Understand
 tone, and storytelling are identical.
This video perfectly articulates what I call the “Audience Discovery Loop” of YouTube Shorts.
Think of it like this:
Upload → Random Seed Test → Engagement → Expansion → Saturation
 ↘ (Flop) → Death
Shorts don’t get views — they earn them by passing mini-tests.
Every few thousand impressions are micro-experiments:
 ●​ If engagement rises → it scales to more users
 ●​ If engagement dips → it gets frozen and replaced by a better-performing short in the feed
That’s why most Shorts blow up hours or days later — YouTube keeps testing them in cycles.
Also, the first 3 seconds is algorithmically equivalent to a title + thumbnail combo in long-form — it
determines if the user stops scrolling.​

🎯 2. My understanding of his deeper strategy
rather than those who obsess over one perfect upload.”
He’s not just giving generic motivation — he’s teaching a data-driven iterative framework that
matches how modern YouTube’s ML model actually trains on creator data:
 1.​ Phase 1: Learning Mode​
 You create a practice channel purely to collect creative feedback data. This bypasses the fear
 of failure and accelerates algorithmic learning.
 2.​ Phase 2: Skill Stacking​
 Each week you focus on one skill — audio, delivery, editing, thumbnails. This is like training
 your model’s dataset quality before going public.
 3.​ Phase 3: Pattern Recognition​
 By observing top videos and analyzing their titles/thumbnails, you train your eye for “pattern
 recognition” — which the YouTube system does too.
 4.​ Phase 4: Content Gap Exploitation​
 You target under-served micro-topics (long-tail queries). These are low-competition entry

So yes — he “broke the algorithm” for 30 days, but not in a way that builds trust, brand, or longevity.

 ●​ Keep the cartoon troll meme visual style, but integrate unique humor or storytelling that
 distinguishes your Shorts.
 ●​ The algorithm loves trends only when they generate new watch time, not recycled meme
 loops.
2. Retention Through Curiosity, Not Fear
 ●​ Instead of “Don’t skip or you’ll miss the giveaway,” use lines like:​
 “Wait till the end — you’ll see something you’ve never noticed in this meme.”
 ●​ This keeps retention ethical and curiosity-driven.
3. Build a Real Retention Arc
 👀
 ●​ Add micro-stories: 3–5 second mini arcs with clear setup, twist, and payoff.
 ●​ Example: “He thought it was over… until the troll face blinked .”
4. Avoid Fake Followers or Artificial Growth Tools
 ●​ YouTube can detect inauthentic engagement patterns (follower velocity without watch time
 consistency).
 ●​ Focus on CTR (1–3%), retention (>70%), and uploads per week (4–7) — that’s the true
 growth loop.
5. Leverage the Data
 ●​ Track each Short’s view velocity (1h, 24h, 48h).
 ●​ Identify when the algorithm “tests” it (the spike moment).
 ●​ Double down on similar structure/content right after that test.
[[PAGE 98]]
6. Use Longform Shorts Bridge
 ●​ Once you’ve built a 50K+ Shorts base, introduce 60–90s “micro longform” Shorts to test
 transition to real storytelling or explainer content.
 ●​ That’s how creators evolve from “algorithmic success” to “brand success.”

💡 WHAT I UNDERSTAND (META INSIGHT)
 algorithmic behavior.
From a technical and strategic view, this video reveals how the 2025 Shorts algorithm works in
layers:
 1.​ Initial Testing Phase (0–1 day)​
 YouTube tests to a small group (based on title, tags, CTR). If retention > 70%, it expands.
 2.​ Acceleration Phase (1–3 days)​
 If audience rewatches or AVD > 80%, YouTube gives it a “push” (short shelf, home feed).
 3.​ Breakout or Flatline (3–5 days)​
 If viewers keep watching past the median point, exponential growth starts. If not, it flatlines.
 4.​ Geography Weighting​
 U.S., UK, Canada, Australia traffic boosts CPM and trust. Low-tier geographies often slow
 discovery scaling.
 5.​ Upload Frequency Control​
 Uploading too fast confuses the algorithm — one video hogs the testing queue, the other dies
 unseen.
 6.​ Ethical Flag Sensitivity​
 AI voice + kids content = automatic risk. YouTube’s new “content classification” AI is highly
 sensitive to cartoon + child-friendly visuals.

🧩 2. What I understand from this video (algorithm behavior revealed)
 publish.
Ben’s tutorial — though mixed with superstition — reveals how YouTube’s algorithm operates in three
🔹 Layer 1: Classification Layer (Metadata Understanding)
hidden layers that new creators often misunderstand:
 ●​ YouTube first identifies what the video is (topic, language, audience type).
 ●​ Settings like category, language, made-for-kids, dubbing all feed into this stage.
 ●​ If metadata is vague or wrong, YouTube can’t match it with the right audience clusters.
💡 What this means: If your content isn’t “understood,” it won’t get tested broadly. Correct
🔹 Layer 2: Trust Layer (Channel Reliability)
classification helps the algorithm “test” it in the right niche (e.g., education, entertainment, lifestyle).
 ●​ YouTube slowly builds a trust score for every channel.
 ●​ If a channel constantly uploads public videos with bad metadata, it may stay “sandboxed” —
 stuck at low impressions.
 ●​ Uploading private first allows backend checks (copyright, metadata parsing, etc.) → safer
 signal.
[[PAGE 108]]
💡 What this means: His “upload private first” trick is really about avoiding negative trust events
(like strikes or broken metadata). Once you’ve built a clean trust record, YouTube tests your content
🔹 Layer 3: Engagement Layer (Viewer Behavior Signals)
more widely.
 ●​ YouTube doesn’t just measure watch time; it measures viewer satisfaction signals:
 ●​ Likes/dislikes ratio (or engagement rate)
 ●​ Retention curve
 ●​ Shares/comments
 ●​ Repeat views or session chaining
 ●​ Hiding your like count can protect early CTR by removing negative bias.
💡 What this means: Even small UI/behavior tweaks (like hiding likes) can psychologically improve

engagement signals that the algorithm interprets as viewer satisfaction.
